To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

cancer patients have an increased energy expenditure and a reduced body cell mass, that energy intake is reduced in relation to energy expenditure, that the energy intake in relation to energy requirement is reduced in relation, and that the resting metabolic rate is increased in relation to energy intake and body cell mass in the cancer patients.

the cancer patients studied were below normal in both body weight and body fat and had an increased energy expenditure and an increased resting metabolic rate, which were not explained by the reduced body weight, the reduced body fat, or the increased height.

(i) cancer patients have an elevated resting metabolic rate and an elevated energy expenditure that is not explained by differences in body composition, and (ii) the energy intake of cancer patients is reduced in comparison to healthy controls, but the energy expenditure is not reduced to the same extent.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the interrelationship between the energy expenditure and intake of the patients with cancer cachexia and the body composition in cancer and control patients.
the interrelationship between body cell mass, energy intake, and energy expenditure in the development of cachexia.
the interrelationship of energy expenditure and energy balance in the development of cachexia and the influence of body cell mass on energy balance and resting metabolic rate in cancer patients.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
in cancer patients, as in healthy individuals, the resting metabolic rate and the daily energy expenditure are closely related to body cell mass.
the resting metabolic rate and the energy expenditure are increased in cancer patients, and that the energy intake is not increased to compensate for the increased energy requirements.
the cancer patients were in a state of energy imbalance.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
in cancer patients the energy expenditure is greater than in healthy subjects of similar body weight.
cancer cachexia may be due to a combination of factors including an increased energy expenditure, an increased resting metabolic rate, and a reduced energy intake.
cancer cachexia may be a metabolic response to the malignant disease, and that the metabolic response is related to the progression and severity of the disease.
The main takeaway from our work is that
cancer cachexia may be caused by increased energy expenditure.
the resting metabolic rate is a good indicator of the energy expenditure in cancer cachexia.
cancer cachexia, a syndrome of weight loss, anorexia, and fatigue, is associated with increased energy expenditure and reduced energy intake.
